20: # Desktop Computer Automation
21: 
22: > **CRITICAL RULES — VIOLATIONS WILL BREAK THE WORKFLOW:**
23: >
24: > 1. **Never run midscene commands in the background.** Each command must run synchronously so you can read its output (especially screenshots) before deciding the next action. Background execution breaks the screenshot-analyze-act loop.
25: > 2. **Run only one midscene command at a time.** Wait for the previous command to finish, read the screenshot, then decide the next action. Never chain multiple commands together.
26: > 3. **Allow enough time for each command to complete.** Midscene commands involve AI inference and screen interaction, which can take longer than typical shell commands. A typical command needs about 1 minute; complex `act` commands may need even longer.
27: > 4. **Always report task results before finishing.** After completing the automation task, you MUST proactively summarize the results to the user — including key data found, actions completed, screenshots taken, and any relevant findings. Never silently end after the last automation step; the user expects a complete response in a single interaction.
28: > 5. **Only minimize windows, never close them unless explicitly asked.** When you need to dismiss or get a window out of the way, minimize it instead of closing it. Do not close any app or window unless the user explicitly asks you to do so.
29: 
30: Control your desktop (macOS, Windows, Linux) using `npx -y @midscene/computer@1`. Each CLI command maps directly to an MCP tool — you (the AI agent) act as the brain, deciding which actions to take based on screenshots.
31: 
32: ## What `act` Can Do
33: 
34: Inside a single `act` call on desktop, Midscene can move the mouse, click, double-click, right-click, drag items, type or clear text, scroll, press single keys or keyboard shortcuts, and work through multi-step interactions on whatever is visible on the selected display.
35: 
36: ## Prerequisites
37: 
38: Midscene requires models with strong visual grounding capabilities. The following environment variables must be configured — either as system environment variables or in a `.env` file in the current working directory (Midscene loads `.env` automatically):
39: 
40: ```bash
41: MIDSCENE_MODEL_API_KEY="your-api-key"
42: MIDSCENE_MODEL_NAME="model-name"
43: MIDSCENE_MODEL_BASE_URL="https://..."
44: MIDSCENE_MODEL_FAMILY="family-identifier"
45: ```
46: 
47: Example: Gemini (Gemini-3-Flash)
48: 
49: ```bash
50: MIDSCENE_MODEL_API_KEY="your-google-api-key"
51: MIDSCENE_MODEL_NAME="gemini-3-flash"
52: MIDSCENE_MODEL_BASE_URL="https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/openai/"
53: MIDSCENE_MODEL_FAMILY="gemini"
54: ```
55: 
56: Example: Qwen 3.5
57: 
58: ```bash
59: MIDSCENE_MODEL_API_KEY="your-aliyun-api-key"
60: MIDSCENE_MODEL_NAME="qwen3.5-plus"
61: MIDSCENE_MODEL_BASE_URL="https://dashscope.aliyuncs.com/compatible-mode/v1"
62: MIDSCENE_MODEL_FAMILY="qwen3.5"
63: MIDSCENE_MODEL_REASONING_ENABLED="false"
64: # If using OpenRouter, set:
65: # MIDSCENE_MODEL_API_KEY="your-openrouter-api-key"
66: # MIDSCENE_MODEL_NAME="qwen/qwen3.5-plus"
67: # MIDSCENE_MODEL_BASE_URL="https://openrouter.ai/api/v1"
68: ```
69: 
70: Example: Doubao Seed 2.0 Lite
71: 
72: ```bash
73: MIDSCENE_MODEL_API_KEY="your-doubao-api-key"
74: MIDSCENE_MODEL_NAME="doubao-seed-2-0-lite"
75: MIDSCENE_MODEL_BASE_URL="https://ark.cn-beijing.volces.com/api/v3"
76: MIDSCENE_MODEL_FAMILY="doubao-seed"
77: ```
78: 
79: Commonly used models: Doubao Seed 2.0 Lite, Qwen 3.5, Zhipu GLM-4.6V, Gemini-3-Pro, Gemini-3-Flash.
80: 
81: If the model is not configured, ask the user to set it up. See [Model Configuration](https://midscenejs.com/model-common-config) for supported providers.
82: 
83: ## Commands
84: 
85: ### Connect to Desktop
86: 
87: ```bash
88: npx -y @midscene/computer@1 connect
89: npx -y @midscene/computer@1 connect --displayId <id>
90: ```
91: 
92: ### Connect via RDP
93: 
94: Use RDP mode to drive a **remote Windows desktop** instead of the local machine. Providing `--host` switches `connect` to RDP and routes every subsequent command (`act`, `tap`, `take_screenshot`, `assert`, `disconnect`) through the RDP helper binary bundled with `@midscene/computer`. The local mouse/keyboard is **not** touched.
95: 
96: Minimum example:
97: 
98: ```bash
99: npx -y @midscene/computer@1 connect \
100:   --host rdp.example.com \
101:   --username Administrator \
102:   --password "$RDP_PASSWORD"
103: ```
104: 
105: All RDP options for `connect` (RDP mode is activated when `--host` is set; the other flags are optional):
106: 
107: - `--host <fqdn-or-ip>` — RDP host. Required to enter RDP mode.
108: - `--port <number>` — RDP port (default `3389`).
109: - `--username <user>` — RDP user account.
110: - `--password <secret>` — RDP password. Prefer reading from an environment variable, secrets manager, or interactive prompt; never paste it into a shared transcript.
111: - `--domain <domain>` — Active Directory / NTLM domain.
112: - `--security-protocol <auto|tls|nla|rdp>` — Security protocol negotiation. Defaults to `auto`.
113: - `--ignore-certificate` — Skip TLS certificate validation. Use only for trusted dev hosts with self-signed certs.
114: - `--admin-session` — Attach to the admin/console session (equivalent to `mstsc /admin`).
115: - `--desktop-width <px>` and `--desktop-height <px>` — **Request** a specific remote desktop resolution. The actual size is whatever the RDP server negotiates back; e.g. requesting `1024x768` against a host that pins `1280x720` will land on `1280x720`. Confirm the negotiated size with `listdisplays --host ... --username ... --password ...` after connect.
116: 
117: Notes specific to RDP mode:
118: 
119: - `--displayId` and `--headless` are **ignored** in RDP mode. A connected RDP session always exposes a single virtual display whose size is whatever the server negotiated.
120: - Two display-listing commands exist and behave differently — pick the right one:
121:   - `list_displays` (with underscore, platform tool) — enumerates **local** physical displays only. Does not accept RDP flags. Useless after an RDP connect.
122:   - `listdisplays` (no underscore, action tool) — accepts the same RDP flags as `connect`/`take_screenshot`/etc. In RDP mode it returns the negotiated virtual display, e.g. `[{ "id": "...", "name": "RDP 10.70.86.26:3389 (1280x720)", "primary": true }]`. Use this to verify the actual resolution.
123: - The RDP transport uses a native helper binary shipped inside `@midscene/computer`. If you see `RDP helper binary not found` errors, the optional `bin/<platform>/rdp-helper` was stripped from your install — reinstall the package or unpack a fresh tarball.
124: - Treat RDP credentials as secrets: do not commit `.env` files containing `--password` to the repo; prefer `export RDP_PASSWORD=...` in the current shell and reference it as `--password "$RDP_PASSWORD"`.
125: - **Latency expectations**: every CLI invocation is a fresh node process, so each command re-establishes the RDP session. Budget roughly:
126:   - `connect` / `take_screenshot` / `keyboardpress` / `scroll`: ~5 s (node startup + RDP TLS+NLA handshake + first frame).
127:   - `act` / `assert` / `tap --locate`: ~5 s + AI inference + any planned sub-actions; expect 8–20 s end-to-end for typical interactions.
128:   - The RDP handshake itself is ~700 ms; the rest is unavoidable cold-start cost in the CLI shape.
129: - **Connect failure diagnostics**: when `connect` fails, the first line of stderr is the actionable error (e.g. `connect_failed: Failed to connect to RDP server: ERRCONNECT_LOGON_FAILURE: Logon failed.`). The subsequent stack trace is diagnostic noise — read the first line, then check credentials/network. Common `ERRCONNECT_*` causes:
130:   - `LOGON_FAILURE` — bad username/password/domain.
131:   - `CONNECT_TRANSPORT_FAILED` — host unreachable or RDP port blocked. Verify with `nc -zv <host> 3389`.
132:   - `TLS_CONNECT_FAILED` — TLS handshake rejected. Try `--ignore-certificate` for self-signed dev hosts, or pin `--security-protocol nla`.
133: 
134: After `connect --host ...` succeeds, the rest of the workflow (`act`, `tap --locate`, `assert`, `take_screenshot`, `listdisplays`, `report-tool`, `disconnect`) is identical to local mode — just remember to pass the same `--host`/`--username`/`--password`/`--ignore-certificate` flags to every subsequent command, since each CLI invocation is stateless and reconnects.
135: 
136: ### List Displays
137: 
138: ```bash
139: npx -y @midscene/computer@1 list_displays
140: ```
141: 
142: ### Take Screenshot
143: 
144: ```bash
145: npx -y @midscene/computer@1 take_screenshot
146: ```
147: 
148: After taking a screenshot, read the saved image file to understand the current screen state before deciding the next action.
149: 
150: ### Perform Action
151: 
152: Use `act` to interact with the computer and get the result. It autonomously handles all UI interactions internally — clicking, typing, scrolling, waiting, and navigating — so you should give it complex, high-level tasks as a whole rather than breaking them into small steps. Describe **what you want to do and the desired effect** in natural language:
153: 
154: ```bash
155: # specific instructions
156: npx -y @midscene/computer@1 act --prompt "type hello world in the search field and press Enter"
157: npx -y @midscene/computer@1 act --prompt "drag the file icon to the Trash"
158: 
159: # or target-driven instructions
160: npx -y @midscene/computer@1 act --prompt "search for the weather in Shanghai using the Chrome browser, tell me the result"
161: ```
162: 
163: ### Assert Current Screen State
164: 
165: Use `assert` to verify that the current screen satisfies a natural language condition. It does not perform UI actions; it checks the visible screen state and passes only when the assertion is true. Use this for validation, QA checks, and final state verification after `act`.
166: 
167: ```bash
168: npx -y @midscene/computer@1 assert --prompt "there is a login button visible"
169: npx -y @midscene/computer@1 assert --prompt "the active window shows a saved confirmation message"
170: npx -y @midscene/computer@1 assert --displayId 1 --prompt "the file picker is open"
171: ```
172: 
173: By default a failed assertion throws an AI-generated reason. Pass `--message` to throw a custom error message instead, which is useful for surfacing the intended outcome in QA and CI logs.
174: 
175: ```bash
176: npx -y @midscene/computer@1 assert \
177:   --prompt "the export completed dialog is visible" \
178:   --message "the export should finish after clicking Save"
179: ```
180: 
181: When the assertion needs to compare against a reference image (icon, logo, screenshot), pass `--image` for the URL/path and `--image-name` for its display name. Each `--image` may be an http(s) link, a `data:` URI, or a local file path. Repeat both flags in matching order when you need to attach more than one image. Add `--convertHttpImage2Base64 true` when the model cannot reach the URL directly. Requires `@midscene/computer@1.9.0+`.
182: 
183: ```bash
184: npx -y @midscene/computer@1 assert \
185:   --prompt "the active window matches the supplied reference screenshot" \
186:   --image "https://example.com/reference.png" \
187:   --image-name "reference" \
188:   --convertHttpImage2Base64 true
189: 
190: # or with a local file
191: npx -y @midscene/computer@1 assert \
192:   --prompt "the visible icon matches the supplied logo" \
193:   --image "./fixtures/logo.png" \
194:   --image-name "logo"
195: 
196: # multiple reference images — pair --image and --image-name by order
197: npx -y @midscene/computer@1 assert \
198:   --prompt "the active window matches both the icon and the logo" \
199:   --image "./fixtures/icon.png" --image-name "icon" \
200:   --image "./fixtures/logo.png" --image-name "logo"
201: ```
202: 
203: ### Record and Assert Transient UI
204: 
205: Use a recording when the state to verify may disappear before a current-screen assertion runs, such as a toast, loading banner, animation, or transition:
206: 
207: ```bash
208: # Terminal 1: keep this foreground command running
209: npx -y @midscene/computer@1 record start --displayId 1 \
210:   --output ./save-observation.json
211: 
212: # Terminal 2, while Terminal 1 records
213: npx -y @midscene/computer@1 act --displayId 1 \
214:   --prompt "click the Save button"
215: 
216: # Send Ctrl+C to Terminal 1 and wait for the saved-path message, then assert
217: npx -y @midscene/computer@1 assert --displayId 1 \
218:   --record ./save-observation.json \
219:   --prompt "a saved confirmation appeared"
220: ```
221: 
222: Pass local display or RDP target flags and `--output` to `record start`, then wait for `Recording. Press Ctrl+C to stop and save.` Keep the recorder as a foreground process in its dedicated terminal; never add shell `&`. Perform the interaction manually or from a second terminal, send Ctrl+C to the recorder, and wait until it prints the saved path before asserting. Repeat target flags on actions and the final `assert`. Optional capture flags are `--interval-ms`, `--max-frames`, and `--watchdog-ms`; `--max-frames` caps sampled frames, and the manifest may contain one additional final representative frame. The default watchdog finalizes and saves the recording after five minutes, while `--watchdog-ms 0` disables that safety limit. The output is a JSON manifest plus an adjacent `<name>.frames` image directory, not an encoded video or archive. The manifest contains relative JPEG/PNG paths and no base64 image bodies. Keep or move the JSON file and image directory together, and pass the JSON path to `assert --record`. Use ordinary `assert` without `--record` when only the current screen matters.
223: 
224: ### Use a Reference Image for Precise Targeting
225: 
226: When the user provides a screenshot, icon, logo, or reference image and wants an exact visual match, prefer `tap --locate` instead of a generic `act --prompt`. Pass `--locate` as JSON. The `prompt` describes the target, `images` supplies named reference images, and `convertHttpImage2Base64: true` is useful when the image URL may not be directly accessible to the model.
227: 
228: ```bash
229: npx -y @midscene/computer@1 tap --locate '{
230:   "prompt": "tap the area contains the image",
231:   "images": [
232:     {
233:       "name": "target image",
234:       "url": "https://github.githubassets.com/assets/GitHub-Mark-ea2971cee799.png"
235:     }
236:   ],
237:   "convertHttpImage2Base64": true
238: }'
239: ```
240: 
241: The same `locate` JSON shape also works for other commands that accept a `locate` parameter.
242: 
243: ### Disconnect
244: 
245: ```bash
246: npx -y @midscene/computer@1 disconnect
247: ```
248: 
249: ### Consume Report Files
250: 
251: The generated HTML report is recommended for human reading first. It includes step-by-step execution details and replay videos for each operation, which makes it much easier to understand what happened and troubleshoot problems.
252: 
253: If another skill or tool needs to consume the report, first convert it with `report-tool` from the same platform CLI package. Prefer Markdown for LLM-based workflows. Use JSON when the report needs to be processed programmatically.
254: 
255: ```bash
256: npx -y @midscene/computer@1 report-tool --action to-markdown --htmlPath ./midscene_run/report/.../index.html --outputDir ./output-markdown
257: npx -y @midscene/computer@1 report-tool --action split --htmlPath ./midscene_run/report/.../index.html --outputDir ./output-data
258: ```
259: 
260: ## Workflow Pattern
261: 
262: Since CLI commands are stateless between invocations, follow this pattern:
263: 
264: 1. **Connect** to establish a session
265: 2. **Health check** — observe the output of the `connect` command. If `connect` already performed a health check (screenshot and mouse movement test), no additional check is needed. If `connect` did not perform a health check, do one manually: take a screenshot and verify it succeeds, then move the mouse to a random position (`act --prompt "move the mouse to a random position"`) and verify it succeeds. If either step fails, stop and troubleshoot before continuing. Only proceed to the next steps after both checks pass without errors.
266: 3. **Launch the target app and take screenshot** to see the current state, make sure the app is launched and visible on the screen.
267: 4. **Execute action** using `act` to perform the desired action or target-driven instructions. Use `assert` for the resulting screen state, or keep `record start --output ...` running in a dedicated terminal during transient-state workflows, stop it with Ctrl+C, and then use `assert --record`.
268: 5. **Disconnect** when done
269: 6. **Report results** — summarize what was accomplished, present key findings and data extracted during the task, and list any generated files (screenshots, logs, etc.) with their paths
270: 
271: ## Best Practices
272: 
273: 1. **Always run a health check first**: After connecting, observe the output of the `connect` command. If `connect` already performed a health check (screenshot and mouse movement test), no additional check is needed. If it did not, do one manually: take a screenshot and move the mouse to a random position. Both must succeed (no errors) before proceeding with any further operations. This catches environment issues early.
274: 2. **Bring the target app to the foreground before using this skill**: For best efficiency, bring the app to the foreground using other means (e.g., `open -a <AppName>` on macOS, `start <AppName>` on Windows) **before** invoking any midscene commands. Then take a screenshot to confirm the app is actually in the foreground. Only after visual confirmation should you proceed with UI automation using this skill. Avoid using Spotlight, Start menu search, or other launcher-based approaches through midscene — they involve transient UI, multiple AI inference steps, and are significantly slower.
275: 3. **Be specific about UI elements**: Instead of vague descriptions, provide clear, specific details. Say `"the yellow minimize button in the top-left corner of the Safari window"` instead of `"the button"`.
276: 4. **Describe locations when possible**: Help target elements by describing their position (e.g., `"the icon in the top-right corner of the menu bar"`, `"the third item in the left sidebar"`).
277: 5. **Never run in background**: Every midscene command must run synchronously — background execution breaks the screenshot-analyze-act loop.
278: 6. **Check for multiple displays**: If you launched an app but cannot see it on the screenshot, the app window may have opened on a different display. Use `list_displays` to check available displays. You have two options: either move the app window to the current display, or use `connect --displayId <id>` to switch to the display where the app is.
279: 7. **Batch related operations into a single `act` command**: When performing consecutive operations within the same app, combine them into one `act` prompt instead of splitting them into separate commands. For example, "search for X, click the first result, and scroll down to see more details" should be a single `act` call, not three. This reduces round-trips, avoids unnecessary screenshot-analyze cycles, and is significantly faster.
280: 8. **Set up `PATH` before running (macOS)**: On macOS, some commands (e.g., `system_profiler`) may not be found if the `PATH` is incomplete. Before running any midscene commands, ensure the `PATH` includes the standard system directories:
281:    ```bash
282:    export PATH="/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/bin:/sbin:$PATH"
283:    ```
284:    This prevents screenshot failures caused by missing system utilities.
285: 9. **Choose the right verification window**: Use `assert --prompt "..."` for the current screen. For a toast, banner, animation, or transition, run `record start --output ...` in a dedicated terminal, perform the interaction, stop recording with Ctrl+C, wait for the saved-path message, then pass the artifact to `assert --record`.
286: 10. **Always report results after completion**: After finishing the automation task, you MUST proactively present the results to the user without waiting for them to ask. This includes: (1) the answer to the user's original question or the outcome of the requested task, (2) key data extracted or observed during execution, (3) screenshots and other generated files with their paths, (4) a brief summary of steps taken. Do NOT silently finish after the last automation command — the user expects complete results in a single interaction.
287: 11. **Prefer `tap --locate` when a reference image is provided**: If the user shares a screenshot, icon, or logo and wants that exact visual target, use `tap --locate` with a multimodal `locate` JSON object such as `{ "prompt": "...", "images": [...] }` instead of relying only on `act --prompt`.
288: 
289: **Example — Context menu interaction:**
290: 
291: ```bash
292: npx -y @midscene/computer@1 act --prompt "right-click the file icon and select Delete from the context menu"
293: npx -y @midscene/computer@1 take_screenshot
294: ```
295: 
296: **Example — Dropdown menu:**
297: 
298: ```bash
299: npx -y @midscene/computer@1 act --prompt "open the File menu and click New Window"
300: npx -y @midscene/computer@1 take_screenshot
301: ```
302: 
303: 
304: ## Improve Precision (Deep Locate / Deep Think)
305: 
306: Two optional global flags help when Midscene struggles with a task. Put them anywhere in the command (before or after the sub-command); once set, the relevant operations use them by default, so you don't pass a per-call parameter.
307: 
308: - `--deep-locate` — spends an extra round of visual reasoning to pinpoint the target element. Use it when an action interacts with the wrong spot (location drift / offset). It applies to every operation that locates an element, including `tap --locate` and the locating that happens inside `act`.
309: - `--deep-think` — plans `act` with deeper reasoning (richer context and sub-goal decomposition). Use it for complex, multi-step `act` instructions; it only affects planning.
310: 
311: Both trade a little speed for better results, and you can combine them.
312: 
313: ```bash
314: # more accurate element location (helps act's internal locating too)
315: npx -y @midscene/computer@1 act --deep-locate --prompt "click the tiny red close button in the top-left of the window"
316: 
317: # deeper planning for a complex, multi-step act
318: npx -y @midscene/computer@1 act --deep-think --prompt "open the Export dialog, choose PDF, and save it to the Desktop"
319: 
320: # combine both
321: npx -y @midscene/computer@1 act --deep-locate --deep-think --prompt "open Preferences and switch to the Advanced tab"
322: ```

324: ## Troubleshooting
325: 
326: ### macOS: Accessibility Permission Denied
327: Your terminal app does not have Accessibility access:
328: 1. Open **System Settings > Privacy & Security > Accessibility**
329: 2. Add your terminal app and enable it
330: 3. Restart your terminal app after granting permission
331: 
332: ### macOS: Xcode Command Line Tools Not Found
333: ```bash
334: xcode-select --install
335: ```
336: 
337: ### API Key Not Set
338: Check `.env` file contains `MIDSCENE_MODEL_API_KEY=<your-key>`.
339: 
340: ### macOS: Screenshot Fails with `system_profiler` Not Found
341: If `take_screenshot` fails with an error like `system_profiler: command not found`, the `PATH` environment variable is likely incomplete. Fix it by running:
342: ```bash
343: export PATH="/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/bin:/sbin:$PATH"
344: ```
345: Then retry the screenshot command.
346: 
347: ### macOS: Screenshot Returns a Black Screen
348: If `take_screenshot` returns a completely black image, the Mac is likely **locked** (e.g. screen is at the login/lock window). This is a system-level restriction — macOS prohibits capturing the screen contents while the session is locked, so there is no workaround at the application level.
349: 
350: **Recommended fix:** Use a **screensaver** instead of locking the screen. A screensaver keeps the user session active and unlocked, allowing screenshots to capture normally.
351: 
352: 1. Open **System Settings > Lock Screen**
353: 2. Set "Require password after screen saver begins or display is turned off" to a longer delay (or turn it off during automation)
354: 3. Optionally configure a screens"}}
